'''''Myrica cerifera''''' is an [[evergreen]] [[tree]] or large [[shrub]] native to North and Central America and the Caribbean. Its common names include '''southern wax myrtle''', '''southern bayberry''', '''candleberry''', '''bayberry tree''', and '''tallow shrub'''. It has uses in the garden and for [[history of candle making|candlemaking]], as well as a [[medicinal plant]].

==Description==
''Myrica cerifera'' is a small [[tree]] or large [[shrub]],<ref name=Chevallier>{{cite book|title=The Encyclopedia of Medicinal Plants|page=236|author=Andrew Chevallier|year=1996|publisher=The Reader's Digest Association|isbn=0-88850-546-9}}</ref> reaching up to {{convert|14|m|ft}} tall.<ref name=FNA/> It is adaptable to many habitats, growing naturally in wetlands, near [[river]]s and [[stream]]s, [[sand dune]]s, fields, hillsides, [[pine barren]]s, and in both [[coniferous forest|coniferous]] and mixed-broadleaf forests. ''M. cerifera'' can weather coastal storms, long droughts, and tropical high temperatures.<ref name=TST />

In nature, it ranges from [[Central America]], northward into the [[southeastern United States]]. Wax Myrtle can be successfully cultivated as far north as the New York City area and southern Ohio Valley. It also grows in [[Bermuda]] and the [[Caribbean]].<ref name=FNA>{{cite web|url=http://www.efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=1&taxon_id=233500790|title=Myrica cerifera in Flora of North America @ efloras.org|work=[[Flora of North America]]|access-date=2008-01-08}}</ref> In terms of [[ecological succession|succession]], ''M. cerifera'' is often one of the first plants to colonize an area.<ref name=USFS/>

[[Image:Southern_Wax_Myrtle_Flower_Sexing.jpg|thumb|250px|left|The male and female flowers]]
''M. cerifera'' is an evergreen. The [[gland (botany)|glandular]] [[leaf|leaves]] are long, have a leathery texture and serrated edges, and contain aromatic compounds.<ref name=FNA/> The plant is [[dioecious]], with male and female flowers borne in catkins on separate plants.<ref name=Chevallier/>  Male flowers have three or four [[stamen]]s, and are surrounded by short [[bract]]s.<ref name=FNA/> The female flowers develop into fruit, which are globular and surrounded by a natural [[wax]]-like coating. The species flowers from late winter to spring, and bear fruit in late summer or fall.<ref name=FNA/> No [[endosperm]] is present in the seeds. ''M. cerifera'' can also [[vegetative reproduction|reproduce clonally]] through runners.<ref name=USFS/>

This species occurs in two forms, but there is no clear dividing line between them, many intermediate forms occurring. Specimens in drier and sandier areas are shrub-like, have [[rhizome]]s and smaller leaves. Those growing in damper situations with richer soil are more tree-like with bigger leaves.

== Ecology ==
The fruit is a source of food for many bird species, such as the [[wild turkey]] and the northern [[bobwhite quail]].<ref name="USFS" />  In winter, the seeds are important foods for the [[myrtle warbler]]<ref>{{cite web|url=https://nationalzoo.si.edu/migratory-birds/news/bird-bound-berry|title=This Bird is Bound to Berry|website=Smithsonian's National Zoo & Conservation Biology Institute|date=15 November 1997|access-date=1 October 2024|last1=Greenberg|first1=Russell|last2=Lowe|first2=Garrett|others=Call recorded by Gregory Gough}}</ref> and [[tree swallow]].<ref>{{cite report|last1=Hardin|first1=Kimberly I.|last2=Evans|first2=Keith E.|title=Cavity nesting bird habitat in the oak-hickory forests...a review|publisher=North Central Forest Experiment Station, Forest Service, U.S. Department of Agriculture|location=St. Paul, Minnesota|year=1977|id=General Technical Report NC-30|url=https://research.fs.usda.gov/treesearch/10095|access-date=1 October 2024}}</ref>{{rp|11-12}}  To a point, ''M. cerifera'' will also provide habitat for the northern bobwhite quail. Birds' digestive systems remove the wax from the fruit, a prerequisite for [[germination]].<ref name="USFS" />

[[File:Starr 031108-0156 Morella cerifera.jpg|thumb|alt=photo|Branch bearing fruits]]

This plant's [[root (botany)|root]]s possess [[root nodule]]s harboring members of a symbiotic genus of [[actinomycete|actinorhizal]] bacteria, ''[[Frankia]]'', which allow the plant to [[nitrogen fixation|fix nitrogen]] gas at a faster rate than do [[leguminosae|legumes]].<ref name="USFS" />

The above-ground growth of ''M. cerifera'' is often killed by [[wildfire]]s unless the fire is very small or transient. In the latter situation, only the most recent primary growth may be incinerated. Because the leaves, stem, and branches contain flammable aromatic compounds, a specimen of ''M. cerifera'' is in fact a [[fire hazard]]. In contrast to the flammability of its top growth, ''M. cerifera'''s [[Root|root system]] is fire-resistant. By 1991, no known fire had killed this plant's roots. However, this plant will not survive repeated destruction of its top growth indefinitely. Three consecutive years of burning may kill all plants affected.

After less damaging fires, new shoots will regrow from below ground. This regrowth is most rapid in the first season after a fire.<ref name="USFS" />

''M. cerifera'' has exhibited aggressive behavior in both native and non-native habitat. On the [[Virginia Barrier Islands|Virginia barrier islands]] within its native range, the shrub has been documented rapidly expanding into grasslands impacting ecosystem function and landscape-level resistance to [[Disturbance (ecology)|disturbance]]. While climate change plays a large role in this, the mechanism responsible is the shrub's ability to alter its own [[microclimate]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Wood |first1=Lauren K. |last2=Hays |first2=Spencer |last3=Zinnert |first3=Julie C. |date=2020-05-19 |title=Decreased temperature variance associated with biotic composition enhances coastal shrub encroachment |journal=Scientific Reports |language=en |volume=10 |issue=1 |page=8210 |doi=10.1038/s41598-020-65161-3  |doi-access=free|issn=2045-2322 |pmc=7237465 |pmid=32427910|bibcode=2020NatSR..10.8210W }}</ref> On the other side of the US, in Hawaiʻi, ''M. cerifera''<nowiki/>'s ability to partner with nitrogen-fixing bacteria makes it a significant threat to native Hawaiʻian forests.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Kurten |first1=Erin L. |last2=Snyder |first2=Carolyn P. |last3=Iwata |first3=Terri |last4=Vitousek |first4=Peter M. |date=2008-01-01 |title=Morella cerifera invasion and nitrogen cycling on a lowland Hawaiian lava flow |journal=Biological Invasions |language=en |volume=10 |issue=1 |pages=19–24 |doi=10.1007/s10530-007-9101-5 |bibcode=2008BiInv..10...19K |s2cid=24211293 |issn=1573-1464}}</ref>

== Taxonomy ==
This plant is one of several ''[[Myrica]]'' species that are sometimes [[lumping and splitting|split]] into the genus ''Morella'', e.g. in the [[Integrated Taxonomic Information System]]. This species also has several [[synonym (taxonomy)|synonyms]] aside from the ''Myrica''/''Morella'' split: ''Cerothamnus pumilus'', ''C. ceriferus'', ''Myrica cerifera var. pumila'', and ''Myrica pusilla''.<ref name=ITIS>{{cite web|url=https://www.itis.gov/servlet/SingleRpt/SingleRpt?search_topic=TSN&search_value=507899|title=ITIS Standard Report Page: Morella cerifera|publisher=[[Integrated Taxonomic Information System]]|access-date=2008-01-07}}</ref> ''Myrica cerifera'' is similar to ''[[Myrica pensylvanica|M. pensylvanica]]'' and ''[[Myrica caroliniensis|M. caroliniensis]]''. These plants' scent or [[fruit]]s can distinguish them.<ref name=FNA/><ref name=CarNat>{{cite web|url=http://www.carolinanature.com/trees/moca.html|title=Southern Bayberry (Morella caroliniensis)|access-date=2014-05-27}}</ref>

The generic name ''[[Myrica]]'' comes from a [[Greek language|Greek]] word ''myrike'', which refers to some fragrant plant (possibly [[tamarisk]]). The specific name means "wax-bearing".<ref name=USFS>{{FEIS|last=Van Deelen|first=Timothy R.|year=1991|type=shrub|genus=Morella|species=cerifera|access-date=1 October 2024}}  Revised 26 February 2018.</ref>

==Uses==

===Food===
The leaves can be washed, dried, and used to season stews or cooking sauces. The berries can also be used as seasoning.<ref>{{Cite book|last1=Elias|first1=Thomas S.|title=Edible Wild Plants: A North American Field Guide to Over 200 Natural Foods|last2=Dykeman|first2=Peter A.|publisher=[[Sterling Publishing|Sterling]]|year=2009|isbn=978-1-4027-6715-9|location=New York|page=174|oclc=244766414|orig-date=1982}}</ref>

===Ornamental===
''Myrica cerifera'' finds use in [[gardening]] and [[horticulture]]. It has been commonly grown in American [[hardiness zone]]s of 11 to 7. ''[[Myrica pensylvanica|M. pensylvanica]]'' substitutes for ''M. cerifera'' in areas colder than zone 6.<ref name=IFAS>{{cite web|url=http://edis.ifas.ufl.edu/ST410|title=''Myrica cerifera'': Southern Waxmyrtle|author=Edward F. Gilman & Dennis G. Watson|publisher=Environmental Horticulture Department, Florida Cooperative Extension Service, [[University of Florida]] Institute of Food and Agricultural Services|date=November 1993|access-date=2008-01-24}}</ref> Since the species is adaptable, it will tolerate many conditions, although it has a need for frequent [[pruning]].<ref name=LSU>{{cite web|url=https://www.lsu.edu/departments/horticulture/plantmaterials/Plant%20Groups/Evergreen%20Trees/Myrica%20cerifera/index.htm  | title=Myrica cerifera|publisher=[[Louisiana State University]]|access-date=2019-07-08}}</ref> It can handle abuse from bad pruning, however.<ref name=NCSU>{{cite web|url=http://www.ces.ncsu.edu/depts/hort/consumer/factsheets/shrubs/myrica_cerifera.html|title=Shrubs: Myrica cerifera|publisher=[[North Carolina State University]]|author=Erv Evans|year=2003|access-date=2008-01-24|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20071122201813/http://www.ces.ncsu.edu/depts/hort/consumer/factsheets/shrubs/myrica_cerifera.html|archive-date=2007-11-22}}</ref> The species has at least four [[cultivar]]s. Those dubbed Fairfax, Jamaica Road, and Don's Dwarf differ from the "typical" specimen in habit and form. The latter two are also resistant to [[leaf spot]].<ref name="NCSU vars">{{cite web|url=http://www.ces.ncsu.edu/depts/hort/consumer/factsheets/shrubs/cultivars/myrica_cerifera-table.html|title=Select Myrica cerifera cultivars|access-date=2008-01-24|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20071204120741/http://www.ces.ncsu.edu/depts/hort/consumer/factsheets/shrubs/cultivars/myrica_cerifera-table.html|archive-date=2007-12-04}}</ref> Var. ''pumila'' is a [[dwarf plant|dwarf cultivar]].<ref name=IFAS/>

===Herbalism===
Bayberry root bark has a history of use in [[herbalism]]. The plant contains several organic compounds, including: [[triterpene]]s such as [[myricadiol]], [[taraxerol]], and [[taraxerone]], as well as chemicals such as different [[flavonoid]]s, [[tannin]]s, [[resin]]s, [[Natural gum|gum]]s, and [[natural phenol|phenol]]s. Myricadiol has a slight impact on levels of [[potassium]] and [[sodium]], while a substance called [[myricitrin]] has antibiotic properties.{{clarify|reason=when applied to the skin?  taken orally? are these effects clinical, or just in test tubes?|date=December 2012}}<ref name=Chevallier/>{{medcn|date=December 2012}}

The [[Choctaw]] boiled bayberry and used the result as a treatment for [[fever]]s. In 1722, it was reported that colonists in Louisiana drank a mixture of wax and hot water to treat severe [[dysentery]].<ref name="Castleman p69">{{cite book|title=The Healing Herbs|author=Michael Castleman|page=69|publisher=Rhodale Press|year=1991|isbn=0-87857-934-6}}</ref> Bayberry was reported in an account from 1737 as being used to treat [[convulsions]], [[colic]], [[palsy]], and [[seizure]]s.<ref name=Chevallier/> Starting in the early 19th century, the herbalist [[Samuel Thomson]] recommended this plant for producing "heat" within the body and as a treatment for infectious diseases and [[diarrhea]]. That use of bayberry waned later in the 19th century, in favor of using it for a variety of ailments, including a [[topical]] use for bleeding [[gingiva|gums]].<ref name="Castleman p69"/> For twenty years starting in 1916, bayberry root bark was listed in the American [[National Formulary]].<ref name=Chevallier/>

Use of bayberry in herbalism has declined since its peak in popularity in the 19th century. The plant is still used today in the treatment of fever, diarrhea, and a few other ailments.{{citation needed|date=December 2012}} The chemical myricitrin has anti-fever properties.{{citation needed|date=December 2012}} In addition, that chemical, along with the tannins, has anti-diarrheal properties.{{citation needed|date=December 2012}} Myricitrin works as an antibiotic, while the tannins have [[astringent]] properties.<ref name="Castleman p70">{{cite book|title=The Healing Herbs|author=Michael Castleman|page=70|publisher=Rhodale Press|year=1991|isbn=0-87857-934-6}}</ref>{{medcn|date=December 2012}}

In general, either a [[decoction]] or a [[tincture]] is used.<ref name="Castleman p70"/> [[Infusion]]s and a topical paste have also been used.<ref name=Chevallier/>

[[Pregnancy|Pregnant]] women should not use bayberry.<ref name=Chevallier/> In addition, [[tannin]] action relating to cancer is unclear, with studies indicating both pro and anti-cancer effects.{{medcn|date=December 2012}} Bayberry, just like any other medicinal plant, should only be used under the supervision of a physician.<ref name="Castleman 70-1">{{cite book|title=The Healing Herbs|author=Michael Castleman|pages=70–1|publisher=Rhodale Press|year=1991|isbn=0-87857-934-6}}</ref>

===Candles===
Southern bayberry's fruits are a traditional source of the [[wax]] for old-fashioned [[Christmas]] decorations called bayberry [[candle]]s.<ref name=USFS/> The wax was extracted by boiling the berries, and skimming off the floating hydrocarbons. The fats were then boiled again and then strained. After that the liquid was usable in [[history of candle making|candle making]], whether through dipping or molding. Southern bayberry is not the only plant usable for making bayberry candles, however. Its close relatives are also usable.<ref name=BTTB>{{cite book|title=Back to the Basics - How to Learn and Enjoy Our Traditional Skills|year=1981|publisher=The Reader's Digest Association Canada|page=372|place=Montreal, PQ|isbn=-0-88850-098-X}}</ref>

Southern bayberry and its relatives have largely been supplanted in candlemaking by substitutes made from [[paraffin wax|paraffin]]. The substitute candles have [[artificial color]]s and [[artificial scent|scents]] that create candles that look and smell similar to natural ones.<ref name=BTTB/>

===Soap===
Wax extracted from boiling the fruit of ''Myrica cerifera'' was also used to make scented bayberry soap by early North-American settlers.<ref name=TST>{{cite book |title=Tropical & Subtropical Trees: An Encyclopaedia |author=Margaret Barwick |page=290 |year=2004 |publisher=Timber Press |isbn=978-0-88192-661-3}}</ref>
